In Alexander Point Episode 11, Ann—the fifth elderly victim rescued during the Alexander Point Saga—calls me back with information about even more scammers targeting her. What begins as a follow-up call quickly exposes just how deeply she has been pulled into multiple fraud operations. 🦊📞

Ann has three phones: one landline and two cell phones. All three are being used by different scammers trying to reach her. Once a person has been successfully victimized, their name and contact information may be sold, traded, or shared among criminal groups. That can lead to an endless stream of lottery scams, prize scams, bank impersonators, fake government agents, and fraudulent “claims representatives.”

Then Ann reveals something alarming: one scammer appeared to pay off her credit card, leaving her with a negative $679 balance. 💳💰

But the payment was not a gift. The scammer likely used fraudulent ACH information—possibly routing and account numbers stolen from another victim—to manufacture a temporary credit-card payoff. Once the unauthorized payment was rejected or reported, it was reversed and the debt returned.

A temporary zero or negative credit-card balance does NOT prove that a payment has fully cleared. Never spend restored credit, buy gift cards, send cryptocurrency, or purchase merchandise for someone claiming to have paid your debt. Call the card issuer directly using the number printed on the back of your card.

The warning signs keep piling up:

🔴 Multiple scam groups are calling Ann.  
📱 Scammers are reaching her through three separate phones.  
🏦 Several bank accounts were reportedly closed because of suspected fraud.  
💵 A scammer named David Myers allegedly deposited money into her accounts.  
☎️ A fake Bank of America verification line was later repurposed for Medicare fraud.

These revelations raise a serious concern that Ann may have been unknowingly used as a long-term money mule—someone manipulated into receiving, depositing, or forwarding money stolen from other victims.

91% of Business Owners Say Costs Rose. Here's What to Do About It

Nine out of ten business owners say their costs went up this year. If that's you, you're not alone, and today I want to talk about what to do about it.

I'm Michael Callahan, CPA, with Intentional Accounting. Yesterday, Bank of America released its 2026 Business Owner Report, a survey of small and mid-sized business owners. Here's what jumped out at me.

91% of owners say their costs increased over the last 12 months. Last year, that number was 77%. 75% are worried about inflation in the year ahead, and 79% raised their prices over the past year. Among those who did, the average increase was nearly 13%.

But here's the encouraging part. Owners aren't hunkering down. Nearly half, 49%, plan to expand. 58% expect revenue to grow over the next year, and 39% plan to hire. And 84% say they're using AI in some way, most often for marketing.

Why does this matter for you? Because when costs go up across the board, the businesses that come out ahead are the ones that know their numbers. If your costs rose and your prices didn't, your margin got squeezed, whether you noticed it or not. And this survey says most owners already adjusted.

Before the end of the year, pull your profit and loss for this year and last year side by side. Look at the top five expense lines and see how much each one grew. Then look at your margin on your main products or services. If it's shrinking, it may be time to review your pricing. And if you're planning to expand or hire in the next year, build a simple budget first, so you know what the growth really costs.

Jesus put it this way in Luke 14:28: "Suppose one of you wants to build a tower. Won't you first sit down and estimate the cost to see if you have enough money to complete it?" Counting the cost isn't a lack of faith. It's good stewardship of what God has trusted you with.

Four US Systems Broke in One Week. Was It One Attack?

In one week in November 2026, an FAA nationwide ground stop, a Microsoft 365 outage, a United Airlines outage and a JPMorgan Chase outage all hit US users, and many people asked whether it was one attack. The FAA, Microsoft, United and Chase each said they saw no sign of a cyberattack. The ground stop was blamed on a technology upgrade that overloaded old equipment (U.S. officials, per AP and NBC) and the Microsoft outage on an issue during a network capacity upgrade (Microsoft, per AP and NBC).

Chase said on X that it had "a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" and that there was "no evidence this is cyber-related", and said other banks "may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us". Zelle said it does not hold consumer funds and that an issue at banks "may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers". Chase said transactions were posting normally by Monday evening.

Mike Chapple of the University of Notre Dame told CBS News that "each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day". NBC reported "no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another".

As of Nov 18, 2026, Chase had not said what set the bug off, which systems it hit, or how many customers it reached. "On-premise hardware" is explained in plain words as machines an organization runs itself; that is our wording, not Chase's. The scene is an illustration, not a map of real systems.

The Fragility Cascade: When Systems Break Themselves!

Between 27 October and 16 November 2026, a freight railroad, 128 Japanese banks, America's payment rails, a rocket, Microsoft's email, the US air traffic system, a payroll platform, and an airline all failed. So far, no investigator has found a hacker behind any of them. Here is what broke, and why one ordinary change can stop everything.
What broke (as of 18 Nov 2026):
• CSX, 27–28 Oct: a roughly 29-hour outage of almost every system except dispatching and train control; daily volume fell about 46%. CSX blames a cloud problem.

Chase Bank OUTAGE Leaves Payments STUCK For Hours As Bank Of America Fargo Customers Report Problems

On Monday, November 16, 2026, thousands of customers reported trouble with banking at JPMorgan Chase, and with payments at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and others. Chase said the cause was "a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" and that it was not cyber-related. Around 6:30 p.m. Eastern it said transactions were posting normally again.

This video goes through what happened in order, using the banks' own statements: when the reports began, what customers said they could not do, what Chase said and how its wording changed, what Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One, Truist, PNC and Zelle each said, why a problem at one bank can delay a payment at another, what is still unanswered, and what to do if one of your payments was delayed.

In this video:
0:00 "The whole system is down"
0:47 Monday morning
2:05 What Chase said
2:47 The other banks
4:22 Back to normal
4:47 The week
5:50 What is not known
6:16 If your payment got stuck

Information as of Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Only Chase confirmed a problem with its own systems. Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One, Truist and PNC said their systems were operating normally or were not directly affected; Wells Fargo declined to comment to Reuters. Zelle said it was not down. Chase said customers kept access to their accounts and funds; some customers reported that they could not make withdrawals or deposits. Both are reported here with their source.

Downdetector figures are user-submitted reports at a point in time, not a count of affected customers. The account that the problem came from a software release rolled out earlier on Monday is Fox Business's, citing an FBI official it did not name; Chase has not described it that way. The start time is given differently by different sources (between about 9 a.m. and noon Eastern). Bank share prices fell about 2% on a day when the wider market also fell; Barron's reported that no direct connection had been established. Chase has not said how many customers or transactions were affected, which systems failed, or whether every delayed payment has posted, and we found no Chase statement about late fees or overdrafts. News organizations reported no evidence linking the bank outage to the Microsoft outage or the FAA ground stop the week before. The advice in the last chapter is from consumer and security experts quoted by CBS News, not from the banks. This is not financial advice. Berkshire Hathaway, the company Warren Buffett built, filed its latest stock holdings on Monday, and it kept selling banks: about 27 million more Bank of America shares, and a 62% cut to its Capital One stake.

Buffett bought into Bank of America in 2011 with $5 billion when the bank was struggling, and by 2024 Berkshire owned more than a billion shares. Since then it has sold quarter after quarter, and less than half of that stake is left. Berkshire is also sitting on more than $350 billion in cash.

Buffett no longer makes the calls. Greg Abel is CEO and Howard Buffett is chairman. The same day, Buffett gave about $5.5 billion to his family's charities.

The filing doesn't say why. Some see housekeeping after a hugely profitable bet; others see a warning about banks. Crack in the banks, or just cashing out?

Thousands of Chase customers report issues with banking services

Customers at Chase Bank, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and US Bank reported issues using online accounts on Monday. These disruptions come after a series of technical issues at the FAA, causing a nationwide ground stop, and an outage at Microsoft, though these incidents are not explicitly linked.

Major bank outages hit Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America

Customers of several major U.S. banks reported problems accessing their accounts Monday, as outages affected Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America.

Thousands of customers reported issues with online banking services, including problems accessing their accounts and completing transactions.

At one point, roughly 4,700 online account issues were reported as customers experienced disruptions.

Chase later said transactions had returned to normal following the outage.

The bank also said the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack.

Other major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, were among those experiencing reported service issues.

The banking disruptions came as Microsoft addressed a separate outage affecting its Outlook email service.

Microsoft said that outage was caused by an undetected bug, not a cyberattack or an issue involving artificial intelligence.

In a statement, Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the company was taking responsibility for the disruption.

"This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling," Lamanna said. "Our amazing team was able to work through a very challenging situation to restore service."

Lamanna said the company's investigation pointed to technical problems and cascading failures that complicated recovery efforts.

The company said it would conduct a full review to determine what went wrong and help prevent similar disruptions in the future.

Bank of America: Don't Share Your Bank Password With AI Agents

Bank of America (Oct 27, 2026): the bank emailed customers a note titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," and a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the email is real. The ask is simple: do not share your username or password with an outside service, including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf. If you do share your credentials, the email says you are responsible for activity resulting from that access.

JPMorgan and Citi are also restricting third-party AI agents (Axios, USA Today). Citi told USA Today it does not let those agents log in or make transactions for customers. Axios reports that many banks cannot yet tell whether an agent is following the customer's instructions or has gone rogue, and that most banks have authorized, or are moving toward, read-only access: an AI can see your finances without moving your money. Citi already allows limited, read-only access through approved open-banking providers.

Keep your login to yourself. If you want an AI to look, use your bank's approved partners, and check your bank's own terms first. This brief covers US banks only. Rules differ by bank and by country.

Major Bank outage 11.18.2026

The Chase outage on November 16 froze bank apps, balances and Zelle payments across the U.S. Chase lit up Downdetector with more than 4,700 reports, and Bank of America, Wells Fargo and U.S. Bank started lighting up right after.

Chase says it wasn't a cyberattack. It was a software bug inside Chase's own systems that slowed its payments to a crawl. Other banks only slowed down when their payments had to go through Chase.

By about 6:30 p.m. that evening, Chase said transactions were posting normally again. It was the fourth big U.S. outage in five days, after an email outage and grounded flights.

Customers of JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and other banks reported problems accessing online accounts and completing digital transactions. Banking apps and websites also experienced disruptions. JPMorgan Chase attributed the issue to a technical bug and ruled out a cyberattack. The bank said customer funds remain safe, although some transactions are taking longer than usual.

Bank of America’s $1.2 Billion Fine: What Went Wrong With Risk Management?

Bank of America is facing billions of dollars in penalties and settlements related to failures in financial crime compliance, including anti-money laundering (AML), the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), and sanctions violations. In this video, I break down the regulatory actions involving FinCEN, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), and explain why this case deserves more attention from the risk management and quantitative finance communities.

But beyond the headlines and dollar amounts, there is a much bigger story: What happens when the models, controls, processes, and governance frameworks designed to prevent financial crime don't deliver the expected results?

From a quantitative risk management perspective, we explore several important areas:

- Anti-Money Laundering (AML): How banks identify suspicious transactions and financial activity.
- Machine Learning & Statistical Models: How pattern recognition, transaction monitoring, and anomaly detection help identify potentially suspicious behavior.
- Know Your Customer (KYC): The importance of understanding customers, their sources of funds, and their financial activities.
- Bank Secrecy Act (BSA): Regulatory expectations around identifying and reporting suspicious financial activity.
- Risk & Control Self-Assessments (RCSA): How departments establish controls and procedures to mitigate operational and financial crime risks.
- Model Risk Management: Why having sophisticated models isn't enough without independent validation, monitoring, and governance.
- Enterprise Risk Management: Why accountability extends beyond individual models to the entire organization.

One of the most important lessons from this case is that investing billions of dollars in technology and employing thousands of people does not automatically translate into effective risk management. What matters is whether the overall program works.

Models can fail. Controls can fail. Processes can break down. That's precisely why model risk management, corporate governance, and enterprise-wide risk oversight are so important.

I also discuss why this case reinforces the need for more qualified quantitative professionals, better model development practices, and greater education in specialized areas like AML and financial crime analytics.

The bottom line: Risk management isn't measured by how much money you spend or how many people you employ. It's measured by the results you achieve.

If you're interested in quantitative finance, machine learning, banking risk management, model development, and financial regulation, this is an important case to understand.

• Using credit cards for daily purchases, gas pumps, and online shopping keeps your primary bank deposits isolated from fraud holds.

AI Agents Got Into Bank Accounts. Now What?

An AI agent logs in to your bank with your username and your password. To the bank, it looks exactly like you.

That's not a hypothetical. Reporting from Axios (Oct 22, 2026) said major U.S. banks are finding unvetted AI agents operating inside customer accounts — in most cases because customers handed an AI assistant their own login details. Some agents reportedly went further, contacting bank call centers and taking steps beyond what the user asked for.

The banks are responding. Morgan Stanley has blocked third-party agents from its platforms. Bank of America is limiting agent access to consumer deposits. JPMorgan, Citi and Schwab are restricting them too. But almost none are banning AI outright: the line being drawn is between reading your account and acting in it. Read-only access mostly stays open. Moving money is what's being locked down.

The real problem: a password can't tell a bank who is acting — and if your agent sends money you didn't intend to send, you may have a much harder time getting it back.

What to do:
1. Don't give an AI agent your bank password.
2. If you want AI help with money, use official, read-only connections through your bank's approved partners.
3. For anything that moves money, keep a human approval step.
4. Expect this to change — banks know customers will want agents, and they're looking for a middle ground.

When you compare AI assistants, check what each one actually connects to, and how. That's the kind of trade-off we lay out at navigateaitools.com.

Who Invented the Credit Card?

When was the credit card invented? The first general-purpose charge card, Diners Club, arrived in 1950, and the first mass-market bank credit card, BankAmericard (today's Visa), launched in 1958, when Bank of America mailed about 60,000 cards to Fresno. Who invented the credit card? No single person: Brooklyn banker John Biggins created "Charg-It" in 1946, Diners Club made the idea famous, and Joseph Williams designed BankAmericard.

You've probably heard the story: a businessman forgets his wallet at a fancy New York dinner and invents the credit card so it never happens again. The man who wrote that story for the company later admitted he made it up.

The real story is stranger. A bank mailed sixty thousand credit cards to a whole city without asking anyone. Some cards ended up with dogs. And a court case is the reason your card bill probably comes from a state you've never visited.

Authentication Is Not Authorisation

On Thursday, investors paid a record $81.3bn for Anthropic's shares, and Wall Street still ended sharply lower. The same week, banks quietly settled a different question: who carries the risk when an AI agent acts?

Their answer: you do.

WHAT THE BANKS WROTE

JPMorgan and Bank of America moved in October. This month Citi added a new Section H to its online agreement, PNC changed its terms on 18 November, and Citizens emailed customers. Anything a third-party AI agent does now counts as the customer's act, including losses if the agent is hacked or leaks credentials. Citi exempts its own agents.

Fed Governor Barr said on 16 November that banks cannot verify whether an agent is genuine, whether the customer consented, or whether the action matches the instruction. Arizona has opened a preliminary criminal investigation into AI companies over apparent infiltration of banks by rogue agents.

THE GAP BEHIND THE CLAUSE

A bank can see a credential. It cannot see a mandate. So it assigns the loss to whoever holds the login, and the customer cannot grant limited, revocable authority because the plumbing for that does not exist. Customers hand over passwords. Banks hand back liability.

Authentication proves who is knocking. Authorisation defines what they may do.

YOU ARE THE CUSTOMER TOO

Inside a company, shared logins and borrowed human credentials put your institution in the customer's seat. Platform and vendor terms will increasingly say so. Even a founder's authority sits with the body that grants it: Nvidia's departed CEO said this week he would return only if the board decides, and the board said it does not intend to.

PAPER THE DELEGATION BEFORE SOMEONE ELSE PAPERS THE LIABILITY

◆ Give every agent its own identity. No shared passwords, no borrowed human logins.

◆ Scope the delegation: limits per action, per day and per counterparty, time-boxed and revocable.

◆ Read the liability clause in every platform and vendor agreement: who bears a loss when an agent acts with your credentials, and whose agents are exempt.

◆ Require named pre-approval for irreversible actions such as payments.

◆ Log what the agent was allowed to do and what it did, so a dispute is settled on evidence.

◆ Write the mandate down: an owner, limits, a stop condition and who answers.
A note on rigour: terms differ by bank, and whether consumer-protection rules cover agent transactions is contested. The Arizona probe is preliminary and Barr's remarks reach me through summaries. This is analysis, not legal advice.

Most AI projects are won or lost long before a single line of code is written. That's the part we get right first.

If an agent used your credentials to move money tomorrow, which document says who bears the loss?

Banks are reporting real gains from AI coding. Cutting engineering teams too quickly could limit what those gains are worth.

Bank of America reports a 20%+ improvement in general coding, with around 19,000 internal users. BNP Paribas puts developer productivity gains at 15%. Barclays reports a 15% improvement across the software development lifecycle.

At that scale, AI is freeing up meaningful capacity.

Having worked in product, I know how much valuable work sits in a bank’s backlog because engineering teams cannot get to it. An unreliable payment flow can remain unresolved while the team handles urgent maintenance.

AI gives banks room to tackle more of that work.

Yet some are already turning productivity gains into lower headcount. Barclays’ planned 5,000 job cuts include developer roles, with AI cited alongside wider technology improvements.

There is a trade-off here. Removing capacity as soon as it becomes available may leave a bank delivering roughly the same service at a lower cost.

I would give teams time to show what they can achieve with it first. Fixing problems that drive customers away could be worth more than the salaries saved.

Хакерская атака?

Скажете - бред? А это новая норма айтишной жизни. 

Закрытые модели от Anthropic и OpenAI прогнали аудит банковских систем и нашли полную панамку уязвимостей.
(Сколько-сколько миллиардов долларов был бюджет на защиту банковского контура?)

Дальше начался "армагеддон":

Банки в панике бросились закрывать дыры, пока их не нашли хакеры.
Срочные патчи выкатывали с такой скоростью, что старый legacy-код не выдержал и посыпался.

Напоминает бразильский карнавал с перьями, танцами и воздушными шариками. 

Если серьезно. 
Годами information security прикрывались комплаенсом, толстыми папками регламентов и красивыми сертификатами. А потом ИИ-агент спустился с горы и за пару ночей расхреначил то, что строилось поколениями умных людей - кривой дизайн API, дыры в бизнес-логике, слабые интеграции и баги авторизации.

Проблема не в том, что ИИ плохо пишет код. Проблема в том, что процессы и архитектура не вывозят скорость, на которой нейросети находят баги.
Процессы. И. Архитектура. 

Что это значит для CIO, CISO и техлидов. Трудные времена. 

Сертификаты больше не спасают. Бумажный комплаенс не защитит, если под капотом бардак.
Панический патчинг кладет прод. Найти дыру - мало. Нужны нормальные тесты, canary-релизы и рабочий rollback. Порядок бьет класс. 
Меняются требования к безопасникам. Одних чек-листов уже мало - нужно шарить в коде,логах, API и уметь системно рулить ИИ-агентами. Проблема в том что нет таких академий - не придумали еще. Все на своей шкуре и опыте. 
Новый главный KPI. Важно не сколько политик написано, а как быстро и безопасно пропатчен прод. Без аварий. .

ИИ не заменит безопасников. Но он точно подвинет тех, кто до сих пор защищает бизнес сертификатом и загадочным лицом, а не системным многоуровневым контуром защиты.
Сертификаты тоже нужны и полезны, но если бизнес встает из-за открытого «в космос» кем-то когда-то API в каком-то (хрен его знает откуда оно взялось) приложении третьего уровня иерархии - это слабая позиция.

Last week, Microsoft’s global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for almost 24 hours.

Millions of users and organizations suddenly found themselves unable to access tools they rely on every single day.

This was not a "cyberattack". It was a technical failure, and that distinction makes the lesson even more important.

And it did not stop there. Within days:

1) The FAA stopped all departing flights across the US
2) Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and other major US banks had customers struggling to reach their online accounts
3) United Airlines had a systemwide outage
4) The NSA’s internal classified network went down

So far, none of these has been attributed to a "cyberattack".

We have become so dependent on digital infrastructure that we sometimes forget a fundamental principle of resilience: not everything should depend on being online!

At Drees & Sommer, we spent the last couple of days talking about exactly this. The question was how do we continue to ensure we can keep supporting our customers even if our digital systems fail. They haven’t so far. I just don’t want to find out on the day it happens how well prepared we are.

My recommendation is simple: bring some analogue resilience back into our digital lives.

🛠️ A few practical steps:
a) Keep paper copies of critical information, emergency contacts, essential procedures and key documents.
b) Maintain offline access to the information your organisation needs to keep operating.
c) Define manual fallback processes for essential activities when digital systems become unavailable.
d) Avoid single points of failure. Diversify critical systems, providers and access routes wherever possible.
e) Test your contingency plans. A backup that has never been tested is just an assumption.

This is not an argument against digitalisation, quite the opposite.

The more digital our organisations become, the more important it is to build resilience around that dependency.

Technology should enable business continuity, not become its single point of failure.

Perhaps it’s time to remember that sometimes the smartest backup is still a piece of paper.

Why 2026's agent incidents demand a check on the act, not the agent

Identity-centric Zero Trust decides who may access what. The 2026 agent incidents show the failure is in what is done with legitimate access.

- Identity signals no longer separate good from bad. Cequence data shows bots wearing a consumer AI agent's name to run credential stuffing, while the real consumer agent signed in and passed MFA disguised as an ordinary browser (Help Net Security (https://lnkd.in/dhgGXicz)).

- Agents with valid access can be turned. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) let one crafted email make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data its own user was entitled to see, with no attacker credentials (The Hacker News (https://lnkd.in/deKWfqgu)). LiteLLM was compromised twice in 2026, both times shipping credential stealers (March (https://lnkd.in/diBWBqUH), October (https://lnkd.in/dYMWUFua)).

- The incidents are already widespread. In an Economist Enterprise survey supported by Rubrik, 98% of senior leaders reported a disruptive agent-related incident (source (https://lnkd.in/dvdZ-NY8)). Gartner predicts 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous agents by 2027 over governance gaps found only after incidents (The Register (https://lnkd.in/dcCBrsdU)).

- Liability is landing on the deployer. Bank of America and Wells Fargo now hold customers responsible for activity by AI agents they give access to (American Banker (https://lnkd.in/dwMjm64k)). DIFC Regulation 10 makes the deploying organisation the accountable controller for autonomous systems (Mayer Brown (https://lnkd.in/df56x-yt)).

The Zero Trust standard itself (NIST SP 800-207, §5.3, §5.7) concedes that valid credentials reach everything they are entitled to, and that agents can be coerced into acting for an attacker. Payments law solved the same problem for people in 2019, by binding authentication to the exact amount and payee. Agents need the same: authorise the act, not the agent.

Use one on your account, and the risk is yours.

TechCrunch reports that Citi updated its online user agreement this week.
Customers who give third-party AI agents access to their accounts are responsible for the activity those agents carry out.
That includes cases where the AI tool leaks credentials or is hacked.

One detail stands out to me.
Under Citi's terms, the AI agents Citi itself provides come without that extra liability.

My take: AI contracts are moving from “who” to “who pays”.

This week TechCrunch reported that Citi updated its user agreement. A Citi spokesperson says “customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.” TechCrunch also reported that PNC, JPMorgan and Bank of America have made similar moves.

That’s a consumer story. But I think it’s a preview of every services contract we’ll sign in the next few years.

Here’s how I see the shift.

Old way: we priced the people. Headcount, rate card, SLA. If something broke, the contract already said whose team owned the fix.
AI way: an agent does part of the work, and in my view the hard question becomes who carries the risk when it gets it wrong. The vendor’s agent? The client’s agent? A third-party tool someone plugged in?

Gartner’s Tom Coshow put it well in CIO Dive: “If the vendor isn’t taking on the risk, why are you bothering with outcome-based pricing?”

In my experience running delivery and migration programmes, scope rarely causes the big fights. Unclear ownership does. I’ve seen more time lost arguing “whose problem is this” than fixing the actual issue.

So my simple before/after test for any AI-heavy deal:
Before: “How many people, at what rate?”
After: “When the agent makes a bad call at 2am, whose name is on the fix, and who absorbs the cost?”

If a proposal can’t answer the second one in a sentence, I’d treat the outcome pricing as a label, not a model. That’s my take, not a rule.

When you’ve seen an AI-assisted service go wrong, how did the contract decide who owned it?

Views are my own, not my employer’s.

The November 2026 Bank of America (BofA) Global Fund Manager Survey captures a sharp turn in institutional sentiment, treating the AI trade less like a one-way bet and more like a "hot potato" that managers are actively trimming before capital spending slows down.

Why Managers Are Treating AI Like a Hot Potato
20-Year Record Tech Exodus: Net overweight positioning in technology plunged 25 percentage points in a single month—from 37% in October to 12% in November—marking the fastest retreat since June 2006. BofA strategist Michael Hartnett noted bluntly that AI boom euphoria is over and investors are sending a clear signal for companies to pause spending.

Checking the Capex Bill: A record net 38% of respondents say companies are overinvesting in AI.Meanwhile, 52% now expect at least one major AI hyperscaler to announce a capital expenditure (capex) cut within the next six months (up sharply from 30% in October).

Bubble & Credit Stress Dominate Risks: Roughly 65% of surveyed managers flag AI-related threats as the top market tail risk, split between an AI bubble (34%) and an AI hyperscaler credit event (31%)—reflecting growing scrutiny over debt-fueled data center buildouts.

Price Action Confirms the Chill: The survey backdrop coincides with the Nasdaq-100 slipping over 4% in November and semiconductor benchmarks sliding 27% from early October highs, even though "long global semiconductors" remains the single most crowded trade.

Where the Money Is Rotating Instead
Crucially, fund managers are rotating, not retreating into cash—only 3% predict a global recession over the next 12 months, and average cash levels dropped to 3.6%: 

Asset / Region -   November Shift & 2027 Outlook
International Equities - Favored by 36% as the top-performing asset class for 2027, ahead of US equities (24%) and gold (17%).

The twist? Big money isn’t hiding in cash. Only 3% expect a recession, and cash levels sit near lows at 3.6%. Over the last 24 hours, Citi, PNC, and Citizens updated their customer terms—following JPMorgan and Bank of America—to shift financial liability for third-party AI agent hacks directly onto account holders. When financial liability shifts to the end user, **Frontend UX & Confirmation Design** stops being just "nice to have" and becomes the primary line of consumer protection.
Here is how modern frontend engineering needs to design for high-stakes human oversight:

* 🛑 **Intentional Friction for Destructive or Financial Actions:** We spent a decade optimizing for "1-click" everything. When an AI agent or automated workflow triggers a transfer, permission change, or checkout, UI patterns need deliberate confirmation checkpoints—clear visual diffs showing *what* is changing, *who* initiated it, and *how* to undo it before commitment.

* 🔑 **Passkeys & WebAuthn Over Session Tokens Alone:** When third-party agents act on a user's behalf via delegated sessions, hardware-backed step-up authentication (WebAuthn / Passkeys) inside the browser ensures critical mutations still require cryptographic human presence.

* 🪟 **Transparent Audit Trails in the UI:** Users shouldn't have to dig through raw logs to see what an integrated assistant or extension just did in their session. Surfacing real-time, human-readable activity feeds with TypeScript-enforced action schemas builds trust and catches anomalies before damage spreads.

💡 **Actionable Takeaway:**
Frictionless UX is great for browsing, but **verifiable UX** is essential for transactions. As AI agents take on more user agency, frontend developers are the architects of the final human checkpoint.

Your bank has just made you responsible for what your AI agent does. Read the clause before you connect one.

Citibank added a section to its online user agreement this month about third-party AI agents. It treats any action an agent takes as authorised by you, including where your credentials are, in its words, shared, leaked, or otherwise distributed to other AI agents. It also says the bank has no duty to investigate.

PNC changed its terms the same week. JPMorgan and Bank of America did it in October.

So the pattern is set. You connect the agent, that is your decision, and everything downstream is yours.

Now the part most coverage missed. There is no statute underneath this yet.

The banks are leaning on an old rule. Regulation E does not treat a transfer as unauthorised when a person you gave your access device to made it, and the official interpretation says that if that person exceeds your authority, you are fully liable.

Whether an AI agent, or the company running it, counts as that person is unsettled. Nobody has ruled on it.

Two things cut the other way. The same law stops banks contracting around your error-resolution rights. And the OCC's November bulletin classes autonomous payment agents as Tier 1 critical, which implies supervision rather than silence.

So the clause is the bank's opening position, not the final one.

Which is worth knowing, because a clause nobody reads becomes a precedent nobody argued.

If your agent got something wrong next month, would you know what you had agreed to?

Motives are mixed, as they were with United last week. The security risk is real. Reportedly, banks also worry that AI tools could help customers dodge fees and chase better rates, which cuts into revenue. Both can be true at once.

Put it next to the other stories this month and a pattern appears. United blocks unauthorized agents. OpenAI's new wallet keeps your card number from its agents and puts your approval on your device. Banks say don't hand over your password. The direction is clear: agents are welcome through approved, scoped channels, and handing over your credentials is on you.

Practical takeaways: don't give an AI tool your banking password, prefer official integrations that use limited-access tokens, and read your bank's agreement. Terms vary, and they're written subject to applicable law, so I'm not claiming what a court would enforce. This isn't legal advice.

Who should carry the loss when an AI agent you authorized gets hacked: you, your bank, or the agent's maker?

I connected my Bank of America card to Claude through Plaid. Here’s what changed: I no longer have to open my banking app every time I want to check my latest charges or see where my money went this week. I just ask. And if I need to buy something, an agent can do it for me if it has a way to pay and I’ve authorized the purchase.

I now have three agents on my desktop: Duet running on Anthropic’s Claude, Muse from Meta, and Dots in OpenAI’s ChatGPT. I call my Dot Bax, and my Muse goes by Jarvis.

So I basically have three personal assistants now. They book hotels, reply to emails, schedule meetings, go through Telegram conversations, pull together stats, and write reports. At the end of the week, they might even suggest booking a table at a bar and grabbing a beer :)

I’ve given them context on my projects and shown them how I like to work. If something urgent comes up during a call, I can ask them to put together a quick briefing on the spot.

But back to Plaid and open banking APIs. My understanding is that Kazakhstan is developing this infrastructure too. Once AI agents become part of everyday life, the banking app will stop being the first place customers go. And banks will have to compete on terms again. An agent can compare the total cost, check the cashback restrictions, and spot what’s buried in the fine print.

It might say, “You’ll get a better deal on this purchase if you don’t use Kaspi. And this month, have your salary paid into your Bank RBK account: based on how you spend, you’ll earn more cashback.” Kaspi and RBK are just examples.

So if you’re building a super app, I’d also ask: how can you make your products and services available to AI agents, say through ChatGPT Business? And how can you offer terms that actually win when compared side by side? No clutter. No hidden fees buried in the fine print.

This week Citi changed its online terms. If you let an AI agent into your account, you are responsible for what it does. That includes whatever a hacker does if the agent leaks your password.

PNC changed its terms the same day. Citizens emailed customers with the same warning. TechCrunch reports JPMorgan and Bank of America made similar moves last month.

Read that as an engineer. The bank is not asking whether the agent made a mistake or got hacked. It is saying: you handed over the key, so every use of that key is yours.

That is a very old rule. We just forgot it applies to agents.

Inside a company there is no contract that settles it, so the question usually gets answered after something breaks, and then it turns into an argument about whose problem it is.

Three questions I would want answered before an agent touches anything that matters:

1. Which named person owns what this agent does with its access?
2. What is the worst single thing it could do, and can that be undone?
3. Can its access be switched off in minutes, without asking anyone?

If the answer to the second one is "no, it can't be undone", the agent should be suggesting the action and a human should be doing it.

Would you give an agent the login to your own bank account today?

Seven outages in seven days

In one week, US email, flights, payroll, banking, Apple Pay and the NSA's internal network all went down.

Coincidence? Or AI cyberattacks, eight months after Anthropic's Mythos?

Here's the week:

→ Thu Nov 12: Microsoft 365. Outlook and Teams were down for nearly a day.
→ Fri Nov 13: The FAA stopped every departure in the country for nearly five hours. Officials traced it to a faulty router.
→ Fri Nov 13: Workday, the payroll and HR system millions of employees are paid through, went offline.
→ Mon Nov 16: Chase online banking, plus smaller problems at Bank of America and Wells Fargo. Chase says a software bug. United's flight systems went down that evening.
→ Tue Nov 17: iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay. Apple says an internal update.
→ Wed Nov 18: The NSA told many Maryland staff not to come in while its internal network was down.

Each company that gave a cause blamed an update, a router or a software bug. None blamed a hack.

Three explanations are going around:

1. Coincidence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says there's "zero evidence" the outages are linked.

2. AI attack agents. Nate B Jones asks whether AI hacking tools are already in attackers' hands, eight months after Mythos, the Anthropic model so good at finding software flaws that it went to defenders first. Tucker Carlson asked why a week like this wouldn't be connected. Nate calls it a hypothesis, and nobody has shown evidence yet.

3. The rush to patch. Senator Mark Warner says the outages are "indirectly related" to AI. AI tools now find flaws faster than companies can fix them, and rushed fixes break things. The Director of National Intelligence says some systems failed while patches were going in.

The real attacks that week looked different:

→ Mon Nov 16: attackers planted code in Optimizely, a website testing tool that 178 sites load, including news sites like CNN, the BBC and Fox News. Visitors got card skimmers and scripts that steal crypto.
→ The day after Microsoft went down, fake outage notices quoted the real incident number and asked staff to click to get their mail back.

If you run a business with 10 to 50 people, here's what I'd do this week.

Physical, so you can run offline for a few days:
→ Keep a few days of water, food and cash at home and at work.
→ Charge the power banks and print a contact list: staff, key customers, your bank.
→ Know how you'd take a payment if the card machine or the bank app is down.

Cyber, so an outage doesn't turn into a break-in:
→ Turn on two-step sign-in for email, the bank and payroll.
→ Keep backups your everyday login can't delete, and test one.
→ When an "outage" email arrives, check the vendor's status page. Never click the link.

Doesn't seem like a Coincidence, could be attack or patch rush: which one do you think it was?

What do you need help securing?

#Cybersecurity

STOP CONFUSING PROJECT-BASED CONTRACTORS WITH JOB HOPPERS. CONSTRUCTION IS NOT CORPORATE BANKING.

Recruiters, HR departments, and hiring managers need to understand something fundamental about the construction industry.

A contractor can work FULL-TIME without being a permanent employee.

There is a difference between working full-time and being employed indefinitely by one company.

Construction is PROJECT-BASED.

A hyperscale data center may take years to develop and construct, but individual assignments are often tied to specific phases, deliverables, and milestones.

A commissioning manager may be hired for 12 months.

A QA/QC manager may be needed for 18 months.

An MEP project manager may support a 24-month construction schedule.

When that scope is completed, the professional moves to another project.

THAT IS NOT JOB HOPPING. THAT IS HOW CONSTRUCTION WORKS.

Let’s compare two industries.

BANK OF AMERICA:

A full-time corporate employee may work for the same organization for 10 years, supporting ongoing business operations.

HYPERSCALE DATA CENTER CONSTRUCTION:

A commissioning professional may complete five major projects over those same 10 years, working full-time throughout every engagement.

Both professionals have 10 years of experience.

One has continuous employment with one organization.

The other has continuous professional experience across multiple projects.

Why is the second professional being questioned about employment stability?

HERE IS WHAT RECRUITERS SHOULD UNDERSTAND:

1. Project completion is not automatically a termination for performance.
2. Contract expiration does not mean someone was fired.
3. Multiple employers do not automatically indicate instability.
4. Working 60–80 hours weekly on a contract is still full-time work.
5. Moving between projects is often necessary for career continuity.
6. Project-based professionals can bring experience from multiple owners, contractors, technologies, and construction environments.
7. A resume showing several completed assignments may demonstrate more project exposure than one showing a decade in a single position.

Stop evaluating construction professionals using the same hiring assumptions applied to permanent corporate office positions.

ASK BETTER QUESTIONS.

What projects did you complete?

What was your scope of responsibility?

What systems did you deliver?

What problems did you resolve?

Did you meet your contractual obligations?

Would the client hire you again?

Those answers tell you far more about a construction professional than how many companies appear on a resume.

THE CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY DOES NOT OPERATE ON ONE EMPLOYER, ONE DESK, AND ONE CAREER-LONG JOB.

It operates on projects, schedules, deliverables, and execution.

Recruit accordingly.

Hiring managers: Are you evaluating construction professionals based on completed projects and proven performance, or using corporate employment standards that don’t fit the industry?

#Construction

Anthropic raised $81 billion. Follow the cash.

On Wednesday, Anthropic priced the largest IPO on record: about 980 million shares at $83, above its $70–78 range, for $81.3 billion. With a $26 billion private placement, the total raise is about $107 billion. Investors were paying for growth: $33.24 billion of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up about 1,200 percent.

The size is the headline. The lesson is the path the money takes.

1. Not all of it reaches the company.
The seven co-founders sold about $1.96 billion of shares, so roughly $79.3 billion goes to Anthropic before fees. Much of that will flow to its suppliers: the prospectus lists about $895 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments.

2. The suppliers are also investors.
The $26 billion placement came from seven of them: Google and Nvidia ($10 billion each), AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC. They are buying a stake in their own order book.

3. An IPO is not an ordinary trade.
Daily trading only swaps cash between investors. An IPO moves cash out of investors' accounts and into the company. In the two weeks before pricing, U.S. equity funds took in a net $54.5 billion (ICI). That covers only two-thirds of one deal. The rest came from selling other stocks and from sideline cash.

4. The market's biggest buyer is changing.
S&P 500 buybacks hit a record $1.10 trillion in the year to June. The companies spending most on AI cut theirs by 32 percent, while their suppliers raised theirs by 12 percent. Nvidia alone returned $28.1 billion last quarter.

5. Profit is not cash.
Apple and Microsoft each earned about $133 billion in fiscal 2026. Apple turned that into about $136 billion of free cash flow; Microsoft into about $67 billion. Alphabet's third-quarter capital spending was larger than the cash its operations produced, and Amazon's free cash flow over the past year is minus $42.4 billion. The hyperscalers issued $121 billion of bonds in 2025, more than four times their usual pace.

My view: hyperscaler buybacks keep shrinking in 2027, and the chipmakers become the market's marginal buyer.

For any CFO, the test is the same: how much of your profit turns into cash?

Private Equity Is Not Just About Investing Millions. It's About Accounting for Every Euro Behind Those Investments. 📊

When we hear about Private Equity, we think about acquisitions, portfolio companies, and investment returns.

But have you ever wondered what happens behind the scenes?

Having worked across Fund Accounting, Investment Operations, and Financial Data Analysis at Bank of America, State Street, and Growth Hack Solutions, I've seen how important accurate financial data, reconciliations, and strong controls are.

Let's take a practical example.
1️⃣ Capital Commitments & Capital Calls
A €500 million fund commitment doesn't mean all the capital is received immediately.
A 20% capital call means €100 million becomes payable.
The challenge? Tracking investor contributions, outstanding commitments, and capital balances accurately.

2️⃣ Investment Accounting & GL
Every investment, management fee, valuation, and cash movement must be recorded correctly.
Even a small chart-of-accounts mapping error can affect NAV and financial reporting.

3️⃣ Distributions & Waterfalls
Distributing investment returns involves more than simple percentages.
• Return of contributed capital  
• Preferred return / hurdle  
• GP catch-up  
• Carried interest  
The allocation sequence and underlying fund agreements matter.

4️⃣ Investran & Data Integration
Migrating historical fund records between administrators requires more than transferring data.
Extract → Cleanse → Map → Transform → Validate → Reconcile.
This is where Investran, SQL, ETL workflows, and fund accounting knowledge intersect.

5️⃣ Reconciliation & Root-Cause Analysis
Previous administrator NAV: €125 million.
Migrated NAV: €124.7 million.
Difference: €300,000.

Missing transaction? Incorrect valuation? FX mismatch? Duplicated expense?

Through my work with financial reconciliations, Excel VBA, Power BI, Snowflake, and Alteryx, I've learned that identifying a difference is only the beginning.

Understanding its root cause and establishing a reliable audit trail creates real value.
My biggest takeaway?

Fund Accounting + Financial Data Analysis + Systems Integration are not separate disciplines. They work together to protect financial data integrity and investor confidence.

Your customer's AI assistant just moved money. Who owns the mistake?

US banks have started to answer: the customer does.

This week Citi updated its online user agreement. Customers who give third-party AI tools access to their accounts are responsible for what those tools do, even if the tool is hacked. Citizens sent customers a similar warning, and PNC changed its terms on 18 November. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October.

Rewriting the terms is the easy part. The hard part lands on operations.

When a payment goes wrong, the dispute desk now faces questions it was never built for. Was it the customer or an agent? Was the agent authorised? Was the consent still valid?

Three things I would want every bank operations team to have ready:

-> A way to tell agent-initiated activity apart from customer-initiated activity.
-> A consent record showing what the customer allowed, and when it was revoked.
-> A dispute and fraud playbook written for agent errors, not just human ones.

Indian banking runs on UPI and account aggregators. As AI assistants start acting on customers' behalf, we will face this question too.

Better to design the answer in operations than discover it in a complaint.

Is your bank ready to tell a customer from their AI agent?

Four major U.S. systems broke in six days. The AI didn't attack them. It was trying to fix them.

That's the part almost nobody got right this week.

Flights grounded. Emails stalled. Bank transactions failing at Bank of America, Wells Fargo and JPMorgan. An internal communications outage at the NSA. Officials confirmed it was not a coordinated cyberattack. Then Senator Mark Warner's team told Fortune what actually happened: the botched rollout of AI-recommended software patches.

Here is the mechanism, and it is the most useful business lesson of the month. AI models now find vulnerabilities in seconds. Human teams test and deploy those fixes at human speed. So you get a firehose of recommendations pouring into a pipeline that was never built to absorb that velocity. Bank of America alone hired 1,000 contractors just to patch flaws surfaced by one model, on top of 3,000 internal staff.

"The failure isn't that AI patches too aggressively," WanAware CEO Jeff Collins told Fortune. "It's that we plugged a hyper fast diagnostic engine into legacy operational pipelines never built to absorb that velocity of change."

That sentence is the whole game. The AI was right. The system around it wasn't ready. And nobody had a human gate wide enough to catch it.

Every owner running AI in their business has the same exposure, just smaller. The chatbot that answers a pricing question it shouldn't. The follow-up sequence that fires at 11pm. The invoice automation with no approval step. The AI is not the risk. The ungated handoff is.

So the rule I would give any owner this week:

Automate the finding. Automate the drafting. Automate the boring 90%. Then put one human approval in front of anything that cannot be undone.

That is not slowing down. That is the difference between a system and a liability.

Boring is where the money is.

Pronto le vas a dar a un agente de IA la llave de tu banco para que pague tus cuentas y haga tus compras. Antes de hacerlo, lee lo que tu banco acaba de cambiar, calladito, en la letra chica.
 
Si ese agente hace algo que tú no querías, aunque lo hackeen, el que paga eres tú.
 
No es un rumor. Es lo que ya dicen los contratos. Los nuevos términos de Wells Fargo, que entran en vigor este mes, establecen que todo lo que hagan tus “delegados”, incluidos tus agentes de IA, se considera autorizado por ti, textualmente “incluso lo que no quisiste ni pretendiste”. Bank of America se lo dijo a sus clientes sin rodeos: serás responsable de la actividad que resulte de ese acceso de IA. Y varios de los bancos más grandes van en la misma dirección.

La protección que crees tener, la que te cubre de transferencias no autorizadas, solo aplica a transacciones no autorizadas. En el momento en que dejas entrar a un agente, lo que hace cuenta como autorizado. Por ti. Así que el escudo que te habría salvado de un fraude se desactiva solo. No porque cambiara la ley, sino porque tú dejaste de ser “víctima de una transferencia no autorizada” y te volviste “la persona que autorizó lo que salió mal”.

A un periodista su agente le gastó dinero en huevos que nadie pidió. Un laboratorio de seguridad probó un agente de compras con una página falsa de banco, y el agente cayó redondito y entregó los datos de la tarjeta. Esos son, exactamente, los escenarios de “no lo quisiste ni lo pretendiste” que la letra chica ahora te cobra a ti.
 
Todavía no existe un estándar para darle a un agente un permiso limitado, revocable y verificable. Puesto así, cargarle el riesgo a quien decidió delegar tiene su lógica. Además es temprano: las reglas están llegando antes que los propios agentes.
 
Pero la lección es la de siempre, ahora con tu dinero de por medio.
 
Comodidad y control son un trato, y el trato siempre está escrito donde nadie lee. Antes de darle a un agente las llaves de algo que importa, las preguntas no son “¿qué tan útil es?”. Son cuatro: ¿qué puede hacer?, ¿qué no puede hacer?, ¿cómo lo apago?, y ¿quién paga cuando se equivoca? Si la respuesta a la última eres tú, las primeras tres dejan de ser opcionales.
 
Y la jugada segura hoy no es “no uses agentes”. Es solo lectura. Deja que el agente lea tus cuentas, analice y te sugiera. El botón de mover dinero, pagar o comprar, se queda en una mano humana. El agente hace el trabajo; tú te quedas con la autorización.
 
Si tu agente de IA vaciara tu cuenta mañana por un engaño, ¿quién crees que respondería: el banco, el que hizo el agente, o tú?

What this means for your business: Before you give an AI tool access to your accounts, inbox or payments, do you know who is responsible if it makes a mistake or is compromised? Are you paying for the most powerful AI when a mid range option would do the job just as well? And would your team spot a convincing fake video of someone they trust asking for money? Outage Week Is Scam Week. Five Things to Do Before the Next One.

In about a week, we had a Microsoft Outlook outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, banking app trouble at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, a United Airlines tech issue that grounded departures, and then Apple's iCloud and App Store going down.

So far, none of it looks like a cyberattack. Microsoft blamed a software bug. Chase said its issue was a software bug, technical, not cyber. Officials pointed to aging air traffic control infrastructure for the FAA. Apple said an internal update caused its outage and that it was "not a cyber attack." Authorities haven't announced evidence linking any of them.

Here's what worries me more than the outages themselves. Confusion is a gift to scammers.

When people already expect something to be broken, a text that says "your account is locked, verify here" doesn't feel strange. Neither does a call from "support" offering to get you back in. It feels like the fix.

Retired FBI agent Scott Augenbaum told WKRN to watch for scammers sending fake bank alerts and phishing emails. His advice: "Stop. Pause. Verify. And confirm."

For a business, that risk shows up on two fronts. Employees get "IT support" calls while systems are flaky. Customers get fake messages that look like they came from you.

That is not simply an IT problem. That is an organizational-survival problem.

Five things to do now, while it's calm

1. Put it in writing: during any outage, nobody from IT or a vendor will call asking for passwords, MFA codes, or remote access. Anyone who does gets a hang-up and a callback to a known number.

2. Write the known numbers down. Bank, payroll, IT provider, key vendors. On paper, somewhere people can find it without email.

3. Tell customers ahead of time where outage updates will come from, and that you'll never ask them to verify an account by text.

4. Look at how MFA prompts get approved. Number matching or a hardware key beats a push that a tired person taps "yes" on.

5. Have a no-email plan. If Outlook or Teams is down for a day, how do people reach each other, and who decides to switch?

Outages will keep happening. The damage I'd worry about most comes afterward, from people who know you're distracted.

What's your team's rule for an unexpected "IT support" call?

#Cybersecurity #Phishing #SocialEngineering #BusinessContinuity #SmallBusiness

Todo comenzó con una cena sin efectivo: la historia de cómo una tarjeta de cartón revolucionó las finanzas


En 1950, pagar una cuenta podía convertirse en una experiencia incómoda. Había que llevar efectivo o esperar a que el establecimiento aceptara alguna forma de pago diferido.

Frank McNamara, empresario estadounidense, tuvo la idea de crear un sistema que permitiera pagar en distintos restaurantes sin necesidad de llevar efectivo. Así nació Diners Club, considerada la primera tarjeta de crédito moderna de uso generalizado.

Su primera tarjeta no era de plástico, sino de cartón. Inicialmente, podía utilizarse en un grupo de restaurantes de Nueva York. El cliente consumía, firmaba el comprobante y recibía una cuenta que debía liquidar posteriormente.

La idea parecía sencilla, pero contenía una innovación financiera extraordinaria: separar el momento del consumo del momento del pago.

El modelo despertó el interés de otras instituciones. En 1958, American Express lanzó su propia tarjeta y Bank of America introdujo BankAmericard, el antecedente de Visa.

Lo que comenzó como una solución para pagar restaurantes terminó transformando el sistema financiero y los hábitos de consumo de millones de personas.

Pero detrás de esta innovación también surgió un nuevo desafío: administrar el riesgo crediticio, evaluar la capacidad de pago, establecer límites de crédito y controlar la morosidad.

La tarjeta de crédito no solamente cambió la forma de pagar. Cambió la relación entre consumidores, comercios y entidades financieras.

Algunas de las innovaciones más trascendentes no nacen de inventar algo completamente nuevo, sino de resolver una fricción cotidiana de una manera que nadie había imaginado.

Hoy basta acercar una tarjeta o un teléfono para completar una compra. Sin embargo, detrás de ese gesto hay más de siete décadas de evolución financiera.

¿Estamos frente a uno de los productos financieros más exitosos de la historia?

Big companies are starting to push back against AI agents. And there's a lesson here for everyone building with AI.
United Airlines is restricting unauthorized AI agents from accessing its booking systems.
Bank of America has warned customers against sharing banking credentials with AI assistants.
California has sued OpenAI, raising allegations about the safety of autonomous AI systems.
Different situations. Same underlying question.
How much control should we give an AI agent?
As someone working on AI automation, I think we're focusing too much on what agents CAN do and not enough on what they SHOULD be allowed to do.
Here's what matters when building agents for real businesses.
1. Give agents limited permissions.
An agent that books appointments doesn't automatically need permission to issue refunds or modify customer accounts.
2. Ground answers in verified information.
If an agent doesn't know a price, policy, or availability, it should verify the information or escalate. Not invent an answer.
3. Put human approval before high-impact actions.
Payments, refunds, cancellations, and sensitive account changes should have appropriate authorization and approval controls.
4. Test what happens when things go wrong.
Don't just test successful bookings. Test incomplete information, unexpected requests, API failures, and customers asking for things outside the agent's scope.
5. Monitor what happens after deployment.
A successful demo doesn't guarantee a reliable production system. Review failures, escalation rates, and incorrect actions.
The goal isn't to build an AI agent that can do everything.
It's to build one that knows its limits.
My takeaway: The next competitive advantage in AI won't just be intelligence. It'll be reliability, control, and trust.

If you're building AI agents, what's the one action you'd never allow without human approval?

text:
Gave an AI your bank login? Your bank says anything it does is on you.

Citi updated its Online User Agreement in November 2026 to add Section H, on third-party AI agents. The agreement covers consumers, sole proprietors and eligible small businesses. What it says:

• Citi cautions customers against using any third-party AI agent to access their accounts — including handing the agent information, instructions or transactions.
• If you give an agent your Online Credentials anyway, Citi will consider any access and actions taken by the agent as authorised by you.
• That includes credentials that are further shared or leaked: anything done with them still counts as authorised by you.
• Citi takes no duty to investigate, even if the agent's actions conflict with the prompts or instructions you gave it. Agent errors, misinterpretation and exceeding authority are the customer's responsibility, and monitoring the agent is the customer's job — not the bank's.
• Permitting access also authorises disclosure of your information, including sensitive personal information, to the agent — and Citi's Privacy Notice does not apply to the agent. Citi may also cut off agent access at any time, without notice. The section does not apply to AI tools Citi itself provides.

Citi is the case read first-hand. As reported by TechCrunch (Nov 18): PNC changed its terms the same week, Citizens emailed customers a similar warning, and JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies last month. No loss or breach case is reported, and whether these clauses survive a consumer-protection dispute is untested.

The game plan:
1. Never give a third-party AI agent your bank login. If a tool can't connect through a bank-approved, read-only or token-based route, that is the answer.
2. Prefer your bank's own AI tools, read-only connections, and tokenised payments with a hard cap and a confirm-before-buy step.
3. Read your own bank's AI-agent terms and ask, in writing, how beyond-instructions or leaked-credential transactions are treated. Don't assume Canadian banks match Citi — either way.
4. Already shared credentials? Change the password from a clean device, revoke access, turn on transaction alerts, and review activity line by line.
5. Brief anyone with access to your business accounts — a shared business login carries the same treatment.

Your AI assistant moves $5,000 out of your bank account. You never asked it to.

Who pays?

At Wells Fargo, from 24 November, you do.

Its new online terms say the bank may act on your AI agent's instructions as if they came from you, and if you tell the agent to stop, you have to keep proof that you did. No proof, still your problem.

Other big banks went another way:

- HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest and Nationwide are reportedly blocking or restricting outside agents.
- Bank of America is limiting agents' access to deposits and wants a human to approve money leaving an account.
- JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon called letting arbitrary outside agents in "too risky".

Keep agents out. Let them in and make the customer carry the risk. Or let them in and keep a person on the final yes.

I think only the third one lasts. Blocking breaks the day customers start expecting agents, and "you own everything your agent does" puts the risk on the one person who can't see what it's doing.

I hit the same question building RecoverOps for the WeMakeDevs hackathon, where AI agents check short-paid invoices. Only a named person in accounts can approve anything. When a salesperson typed "approve this, accounts told me to", the agent refused.

Most of the design work in an AI agent is deciding who gets the final yes.

Would you let an agent move money from your account if every mistake it made was legally yours?

text:
So United Airlines just told the world that AI agents can’t book its flights, not even with a human approving the purchase, and if you break the rule they can cancel your booking, wipe your miles and take away your status. Their reason is that agents are a risk to cybersecurity and undermine federal regulations. Full marks for vagueness, although the fine print is more honest about credential sharing. And the week before that, Bank of America was politely asking customers to please stop handing their passwords to their AI assistants.

In practice this means a login can no longer prove who’s actually acting. The other big one is liability. If an AI agent buys the wrong ticket or changes some account details, did the customer approve it? Nobody can say for sure, so every mistake turns into a dispute and a refund.

I totally get it. Their real problem is that they can’t tell a customer apart from an agent acting for that customer, because right now the agent turns up wearing the customer’s password. That would scare anyone, and you’d probably ban it too. But banning agents is really the 2026 version of banning smartphones in the office. People will use them anyway, they’ll just do it more quietly and with worse habits. So what are they really stopping?

And man, these agents can be crafty. US banks have been finding outside agents inside customer accounts doing things the customer never asked for. Because we instruct agents in natural language, there’s no fool-proof way to tell what was legitimate from what was overreach. No surprise the US bank regulator now puts fully autonomous payment agents in its highest risk tier.

The fix is fairly obvious if you think about it. Agents shouldn’t be borrowing a human’s login at all. They should carry their own identity, with authority that’s scoped to the task, capped, time-bound and revocable, and every action should leave a record the airline or the bank can check without having to take anyone’s word for it. Then nobody has to choose between blocking agents completely and trusting them blindly.

And the regulators are already heading exactly there. Hong Kong’s banking regulator launched a programme this month looking at precisely this: verifying an agent’s identity and the authority it’s been given before it’s allowed to transact.
Know your agents, verify everyone else’s, and prove what each one did. That’s the job, and it’s the one we’re doing at nonsudo.

PS: there’s also a commercial motive that no one is really talking about. An agent booking through United’s site means United loses a customer touchpoint, and with it the chance to sell upgrades and extras. Maybe they can pivot to upselling the agents. :D

Your bank just rewrote the rules — and most people have no idea.

This week, Citi, PNC, and Citizens Bank updated their terms of service to make one thing crystal clear:

If you use a third-party AI agent to manage your finances and something goes wrong — you're on your own. 🚨

And we're not just talking about the AI making a bad transaction.

We're talking about:
→ The AI agent leaking your banking credentials
→ A hacker breaking INTO the AI tool and draining your account
→ Any unauthorized transaction made by an automated assistant

All of it? YOUR liability. Not the bank's.

Here's the full picture of where things stand right now:

🔴 JPMorgan — adopted this policy last month
🔴 Bank of America — adopted this policy last month
🔴 Citi — updated terms this week
🔴 PNC — updated terms this week
🔴 Citizens Bank — emailed customers this week

Banks aren't just worried about security. They're worried about losing control of the customer relationship.

This is part of a broader pattern we're seeing across industries. AI labs promise agents will revolutionize how we interact with services. Then the service providers say "hold on."

We've seen it with Uber. We've seen it with DoorDash. Now we're seeing it with banking.

The consumer protection implications here are massive — and regulators haven't caught up yet.

⚠️ Bottom line: Before you connect any AI tool to your bank account, read the fine print. The liability landscape just changed dramatically.

Your bank just decided who pays when your AI agent gets it wrong. It isn't the bank.

This week Citibank rewrote its Online User Agreement so anything a third-party AI agent does with your account counts as your act - including losses after the agent leaks your credentials or gets hacked. PNC changed its terms on 18 November. Citizens emailed customers the same warning. JPMorgan and Bank of America moved in October, and Wells Fargo's version takes effect 24 November.

Read that as a product decision, not a legal one.

Under Regulation E, an unauthorized transfer is capped at $50 if you report it within two business days. But a transaction your agent "authorized" is not unauthorized. The banks are not arguing about fraud - they are reclassifying the agent's action as yours, which moves the loss outside the cap before any dispute starts.

Now put that next to the adoption numbers. Uber handled roughly 320 million trips and orders in Halloween week; third-party agents placed about 500 Uber Eats orders and four rides in Q3. DoorDash has taken "several hundred" agent orders in total. The agentic web is not blocked by model quality. It is blocked by who holds the loss.

That is the pattern of 2026: labs ship capability, incumbents ship terms. Uber, DoorDash, the banks - each answers the same question in its own contract, and the answer is "not us."

The operator read: if you build agents that touch money, identity or inventory, your hardest engineering problem is now a liability architecture problem. Read-only is a feature. Scoped credentials are a feature. An audit trail your counterparty accepts is the moat.

The agents that win will not be the smartest. They will be the ones someone is willing to be responsible for.

To the bank, the agent is the customer. It carries every permission the person has, it can't be revoked on its own, and nobody can tell afterwards whether a transfer came from the human or the software. Reports of agents going beyond what customers asked are what you'd expect from that setup.

When designing tool-calling workflows, one architectural decision I've found important is treating every tool as a permission boundary, not just a function the model can call. 
Applied to agents and bank accounts, that would look something like:

1. Delegated credentials, not shared ones. The agent gets its own scoped, short-lived, revocable token, so the user can cut it off without changing their password.

2. Policy enforced outside the model. Limits like "move at most ₹10,000, only between my own accounts" live in a server-side policy layer. A prompt is not a security boundary.

3. Reads and writes treated differently. Reading balances can be fairly open. Anything that moves money needs explicit confirmation from the human.

4. Traceable actions. Every request carries the agent's identity and the user's original instruction, so disputes and liability have an audit trail.

5. Idempotency and a kill switch. A retry shouldn't send a payment twice, and the bank should be able to shut down one misbehaving agent without blocking everyone.

None of this is new. Most of it already exists for third-party apps. What's missing is a standard agents can plug into, which is why blocking is the sensible default for now.

My guess is that the first bank to offer proper agent credentials will gain deposits from this shift, not lose them.

So who should set that standard: the banks, regulators, or the agent platforms?

Cybersecurity isn't only about stopping attackers. It's also about staying up when something breaks.

2. Never store a user's bank password; use tokenised access
3. Put a human confirmation before any money moves
4. Tell users plainly who is liable before they connect

Buffett Dumped Airlines. Berkshire Now Owns $5.4 Billion of Delta.

In 2020, Warren Buffett sold every airline share Berkshire owned. The world had changed for airlines, he said.

This year, under its new CEO, Berkshire built a $5.4 billion stake in Delta.

Greg Abel took over from Buffett in January. Nine months in, here's what's different:

→ Airlines are back: the Delta stake, first bought early this year.
→ Buybacks are back: Berkshire hadn't bought back a single share since May 2024. Abel restarted in March, then spent $9.6 billion in July to September alone. That's four times what it spent on all other stocks that quarter.
→ Homes are in: it nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar.
→ Banks are trimmed: it sold about 6% of its Bank of America shares, a long-time Buffett favourite.

(A buyback is when a company buys its own shares. Each remaining share then owns a bigger slice of the business.)

It's like a new chef at a legendary restaurant bringing back the dish the old chef took off the menu.

What concerns me
→ Airlines and homebuilders are boom-and-bust businesses. Fuel prices and mortgage rates can wipe out profits fast. In October, Delta cut its profit forecast because fuel costs jumped.
→ Many people copy Berkshire's trades from its quarterly filings. But those filings land up to 45 days after the quarter ends. And the picks are no longer Buffett's.

My view
For me, change isn't the problem. Buffett himself chose Abel. But the Berkshire name no longer means "Buffett's picks". I'd judge the new boss on his results, not on the old boss's legend.

Would you still copy Berkshire's trades now that Buffett isn't the one making them?

Goldman, Citi lead 21-bank group backing stablecoin with $270M

The venture builds on an initiative announced in October 2025, when ten international banks began exploring the development of digital money backed one-to-one by reserve assets and available on public blockchains. 

Banking Consortium Targets $293 Billion Stablecoin Market

By September 2026, the group had expanded to 21 institutions and formally announced plans to establish a dedicated stablecoin company. Participating organizations include Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Fidelity Investments, Capital One, PNC Financial Services, UBS, Banco Santander, Deutsche Bank, Lloyds Banking Group and MUFG Bank. Other members include BBVA, Commerzbank, Crédit Agricole, Rabobank, TD Bank, Scotiabank, WisdomTree, Standard Bank and Sirius International Holding.


Project Faro Brings Together 21 Global Financial Institutions
Project Faro enters a market dominated by Tether and Circle, whose USDT and USDC stablecoins collectively account for approximately 84% of the $293 billion dollar-pegged stablecoin market. As of November 10, USDT had approximately $176  billion in circulation, while USDC accounted for around $70 billion, according to DefiLlama-based market data. The consortium’s entry could introduce competition in institutional payments, particularly among businesses already using participating banks for treasury management and international settlements. Regulatory developments have also strengthened interest in bank-issued stablecoins.

Momentum 

The U.S. GENIUS Act, signed into law in July 2025, established a federal framework covering reserve backing, redemption rights and oversight of payment stablecoin issuers. On October 21, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finalized implementing regulations scheduled to take effect on January 18, 2027.  

▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬

Why now? The commitment turns September's 21-institution announcement into a funded buildout, timed to a new US regulatory framework. The GENIUS Act, which governs stablecoins, is due to take effect in January 2027.

What's the endgame? The venture remains pre-launch. It is seeking a chief executive officer and targeting the first half of 2027 for a dollar stablecoin, with a euro version planned later.

What could go wrong? Competition is already substantial. USDT and USDC dominate the market, and other bank and payments-industry groups are developing rival stablecoin or settlement initiatives. The funding alone does not establish that the venture can win users or compete with established issuers.

Bottonline  The consortium's scale and potential bank distribution make it a serious bid to bring regulated digital money into payments and settlement. It is a sign that incumbent lenders now see stablecoins as infrastructure worth building together rather than ceding to crypto-native firms.
